newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers keep up pressure as talks go on.
newsitem.headline: French truckers keep up pressure as talks go on.

text.p: Striking truckers tightened their stranglehold on the French economy on Wednesday as union leaders and employers hinted at progress in marathon negotiations that went on through the night for the third consecutive day.
Sources close to the talks said an agreement may be near on at least one key point of contention on the tenth day of the most serious labour unrest to hit France this year.
The truckers are seeking higher pay, shorter hours and retirement at 55 instead of 60, and the sources said a compromise was in sight on the retirement issue.
One government observer said a broader agreement might be within reach later in the day in the negotiations which began at 3 p.m. (1400 GMT) on Tuesday.
Truckers, meanwhile, kept up nearly 200 barricades on roads and around refineries and petrol depots across France in a protest that was starting to cut deeply into economic activity.

Some factories were forced to close their doors because they could not obtain raw materials while farmers reported spot shortages in animal feed as grain shipments were prevented from reaching feed processors.

Wednesday was also a test of wider union disaffection in France. The big Communist-led CGT union has urging workers to rally at the truckers' barricades to express support and step up pressure on Prime Minister Alain Juppe to drop austerity policies.
Pilots, stewards and engineers at French airlines mounted a parallel two-day strike early in the day, forcing state airline Air France to cut back on its flight schedule.
A spokesman said Air France planned to provide two-thirds of long-haul and just a quarter of medium-haul flights due to the union protest over feared job cuts and restructurings.

The airline's short-haul unit Air France Europe, which operates mainly domestic routes, expected to cut more than half its flights. It said it would guarantee 213 flights on Wednesday and 200 on Thursday, against 480 normally each day.
On the railways, three unions were staging a 24-hour strike from Tuesday evening at the Sotteville-les-Rouen depot in northwest France, a symbolic bastion during last year's strikes.

The barricades around refineries and fuel depots were forcing the closure of some petrol stations, and petrol rationing has been imposed in some parts of the country so that supplies could be maintained for fire engines and ambulances.
The strike was also starting to disrupt mail, grain imports and angering foreign truckers blocked on French roads.

Police were deployed around the Transport Ministry after a call by three taxi drivers' unions to "join the truckers" and demonstrate for their own demands. Half a dozen taxis turned up early on Wednesday.

The French franc stayed under pressure as traders said markets feared the strike could spread, or that the government would agree to the strikers' demands and encourage costly copycat strikes in other sectors.
CGT union boss Louis Viannet planned to meet striking truckers at Saint-Pol-de-Mer in northern France near a blocked refinery to show his support for their movement.

And the Force Ouvriere union, which led a 24-day wave of anti-government strikes with the CGT that virtually paralysed France in late 1995, has also said it was considering widening the strikes to public transport.
